actions.justification: Mandatory first step - continuous monitoring of HR, BP, SpO2, and RR to assess hemodynamic stability and guide management of suspected PE.
Mandatory - Wells score is the standard clinical prediction rule for PE probability stratification. Patient has pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, which are key PE criteria.
Mandatory - D-dimer is the first-line lab test for PE workup. If low Wells score + negative D-dimer, PE can be excluded without imaging.
12-lead ECG should be obtained within 10 minutes of presentation per AHA guidelines to evaluate for STEMI and other cardiac causes of chest pain. Also helps rule out RV strain pattern in PE.
Patient presenting with acute dyspnea; supplemental oxygen supports oxygenation while diagnostic workup proceeds, though SpO2 is currently 98%.
Patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with completed Wells score assessment warrants pulmonology consultation to assist with PE workup and management planning.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Wells score has been assessed and D-dimer ordered, making CT pulmonary angiography the next critical step to confirm or rule out pulmonary embolism per PE workup guidelines.

Chest X-ray should be obtained to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) contributing to acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, as recommended in initial chest pain assessment guidelines.
Echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, which would indicate hemodynamically significant PE and guide risk stratification and treatment decisions.

A 12-lead ECG is indicated per AHA guidelines for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI/ST changes and RV strain pattern suggestive of PE. Although a prior ECG was ordered, 'order_imaging_ecg' is a distinct available action in this scenario and provides current cardiac electrical assessment.

Lower extremity venous duplex ultrasound is indicated to evaluate for DVT as part of the workup for suspected pulmonary embolism (acute dyspnea + pleuritic chest pain), complementing the CT-PA already ordered.
Echocardiogram (bedside) can assess for RV strain/dilation and hemodynamic impact of possible PE, helping risk-stratify the patient and guide management decisions.

ABG provides assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, helping to characterize severity and guide management for suspected PE.
BNP/NT-proBNP helps assess right heart strain, which is relevant in suspected pulmonary embolism and aids in risk stratification for PE severity.
Basic metabolic panel assesses renal function (important before contrast CT-PA if not already done), electrolytes, and baseline metabolic status.

CBC is not yet completed and provides important baseline data including WBC (infection/inflammation), hemoglobin (anemia contributing to dyspnea), and platelet count (relevant before anticoagulation for suspected PE).
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are essential before initiating anticoagulation therapy for suspected pulmonary embolism, and help assess baseline clotting status.
Lactate level helps assess tissue perfusion and identify occult hemodynamic compromise or right heart strain in the setting of suspected PE, even with currently stable vitals.

Troponin is indicated per AHA chest pain guidelines for risk stratification in acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. It also helps assess for right heart strain in suspected pulmonary embolism, which is consistent with this patient's presentation. This has not yet been completed.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with high clinical suspicion for pulmonary embolism (extensive workup already ordered including CT-PA). Per PE guidelines, empiric anticoagulation with LMWH should be initiated in patients with intermediate-to-high clinical probability while awaiting imaging confirmation, provided no contraindications exist. Patient is hemodynamically stable, making LMWH the preferred agent over thrombolysis or vasopressors.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, consistent with suspected pulmonary embolism. LMWH has been given; continuing anticoagulation (e.g., transitioning or confirming therapeutic anticoagulation) is appropriate while awaiting CT-PA results. This is the guideline-recommended treatment for suspected PE with stable hemodynamics (SpO2 98%, HR 80, BP 120/80).

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, highly suggestive of pulmonary embolism. Extensive workup including CT-PA, D-dimer, Wells score, and LMWH have been initiated. Systemic anticoagulation with IV heparin is appropriate to ensure adequate therapeutic anticoagulation coverage while awaiting CT-PA confirmation, especially given the clinical suspicion for PE and stable hemodynamics.

Patient with suspected PE (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain) who has received anticoagulation. IV fluid support can help maintain preload in the setting of right ventricular strain from PE. Vitals are currently stable (BP 120/80, HR 80), but cautious fluid resuscitation is appropriate supportive care while awaiting CT-PA results and further workup.

Patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with extensive workup already completed including CT-PA ordered. Given concern for pulmonary embolism, consulting interventional radiology is appropriate in case catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy is needed, especially if CT-PA confirms massive/submassive PE. Patient is currently hemodynamically stable (BP 120/80, HR 80, SpO2 98%) so systemic thrombolysis is not yet indicated, but early IR consultation prepares for escalation if needed.
